note_on_method: Nobody working on this has played on these courts. Every sentence below is drawn from a Town of Cary page listed in this file, and because the town states its court counts in prose rather than a table, each count is quoted in the town's own words. Where a page is silent, on surface at all three parks and on lighting at two of them, the note says so rather than guessing.

slots.description:
The Neighborhood Park on McCrimmon Parkway is the largest pickleball site in Cary and the only one the town describes as lit. Its features list is precise about the difference between its two racquet sports: "Lighted Tennis Court: Reservable 16 hours in advance" sits directly above "Lighted Pickleball Courts: Non-reservable, first-come, first-served". The sport you can book here is tennis. For a player turning up unannounced that is the better deal, because nobody can have reserved the pickleball courts out from under you.

The court count comes from a different page. The park's own entry confirms the courts exist and are lit but gives no number, while the Cary Tennis Park facility page lists this site among its satellite locations as "McCrimmon Park (3870 Cary Glen Blvd.) Six Lighted Tennis Courts and Six Lighted Pickleball Courts". Six is the published figure.
slots.getting_there: 3870 Cary Glen Blvd, at the south-east corner of Green Level Church Road and McCrimmon Parkway in north-west Cary. The town publishes no parking guidance for this park: no lot location, no capacity, no time limit. That is a gap worth knowing at the busiest pickleball site in town. Restrooms are listed among the park's features, and paved loop trails run through the 20-acre site.
slots.what_to_expect:
Six lighted courts, first-come and first-served, with no way to reserve them. This is where Cary runs its Monday evening open play, 7 to 9 p.m., and the town's leagues use these courts periodically for match play, so an evening visit may find a league on.

Park hours are sunrise to sunset, extended in lighted areas where visitors are taking part in an approved extended-use activity until thirty minutes after it ends or 11 p.m., whichever comes first. The extension is tied to an approved activity, not to casual play, so lights do not automatically mean a late game. No surface material, nets or fee is published for this venue.

faqs.q: Is this the same place as McCrimmon Park?
faqs.a: Yes. The town's own park page calls it the Neighborhood Park on McCrimmon Parkway; its Cary Tennis Park page calls it McCrimmon Park. The park's own name is the one published here, with the shorter one kept as an alias.

slots.description:
The Town of Cary points to Ed Yerha Park first. Its page opens by saying the park "features Cary's outdoor Pickleball courts, where everyone is welcome and encouraged to play". There are three of them, stated plainly in the features list as "Three pickleball courts", alongside one basketball slab and one open play field.

For a player this is a small, straightforward, purpose-signposted venue rather than a large one: three courts, restrooms and a picnic shelter, at the park the town describes as the home of its outdoor pickleball. It was formerly White Oak Park.
slots.getting_there: 1216 Jenks Carpenter Road. The town publishes no parking information for this park at all, not a lot, not a capacity, not a restriction, so all anyone can tell you is that the page does not say. Restrooms are on site and the town's status board lists them as open. There is a picnic shelter, available by reservation, and a playground.
slots.what_to_expect:
Three courts on a first-come, first-served basis. The town's own status board for the park reads "Pickleball Courts Open - First Come, First Served", and there is no reservation system for them.

Come in daylight. The park's hours are published as "Sunrise to Sunset" flatly, with none of the extended-activity clause that Carpenter Park and the McCrimmon Parkway park carry, and nothing on the page states that these courts are lit, so lighting is recorded as not stated. The basketball slab is listed separately from the pickleball courts, which suggests the two are not sharing a surface here, though the town does not say so outright. No surface, no nets and no fee are published for this venue.

faqs.q: Is this the same as White Oak Park?
faqs.a: Yes. Ed Yerha Park is the former White Oak Park, renamed for Ed Yerha, a councilmember who served from 2012 to 2022 and volunteered for Cary for more than two decades. The town's own page explains the change, and its open data still carries the old name on the same map point, which is how the two records were matched to one place.

slots.description:
Carpenter Park is a 16-acre neighbourhood park in north-west Cary whose three pickleball courts share their surface with basketball. The town states it directly in the features list: "Multi-Sport Courts: Basketball & 3 Pickleball Courts". That is a useful piece of honesty. You are playing on multi-sport slabs, and the lines under your feet are not all yours.

The park is also the memorial site for Flights AE3379 and AE3378, and it holds a central pond with an earthen dam, a community garden, a terraced lawn, preserved forest and pedestrian trails.
slots.getting_there: 4420 Louis Stephens Drive, and the town publishes "Parking for 30 Cars". That is the only parking capacity any operator in this directory has given us, and it is worth reading against what else is at the park: a playground, a community garden, a picnic shelter, trails and a memorial all draw on the same thirty spaces as the courts. There is a restroom structure on site. No time limit, permit requirement or fee is published for the parking.
slots.what_to_expect:
Three courts, shared with basketball, on multi-sport slabs. Expect that sharing to matter: a basketball game has as much claim on the surface as you do, and with three courts a queue builds quickly at a neighbourhood park this size.

Park hours are sunrise to sunset, extended in lighted areas where visitors are taking part in an approved extended-use activity until thirty minutes after it ends or 11 p.m. at the latest. The picnic shelter at the playground is first-come, first-served rather than reservable. No surface material, nets or fee is published for the courts.

faqs.q: Can I play here after dark?
faqs.a: Not on anything the town has published. The extension to park hours applies only in lighted areas during approved extended-use activities, and the page does not state that the pickleball courts themselves are lit, so lighting here is recorded as not stated. Of Cary's three parks, only the Neighborhood Park on McCrimmon Parkway has lighted pickleball courts stated outright.
